lesson.title: Calculus: second derivatives, monotonic functions and maxima-minima

coverage.section: Higher order derivatives (up to second order)
Higher order derivatives (up to second order)

blocks.text: Higher order derivatives (up to second order)

If $y=f(x)$ is differentiable, its derivative $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f'(x)$ is again a function of $x$. Differentiating it once more gives the **second order derivative** $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=f''(x)$. It measures how fast the slope itself changes (the rate of change of the rate of change).
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=f''(x)$. It exists wherever $f'$ is differentiable. Other notations are $y''$, $y_2$ and $D^2y$.

blocks.problem: If $y=x^3\log x$, find $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ and its value at $x=e$.
blocks.solution:
Product rule: $y'=3x^2\log x+x^3\cdot\tfrac1x=3x^2\log x+x^2$.

Differentiate again: $y''=6x\log x+3x^2\cdot\tfrac1x+2x=6x\log x+3x+2x=6x\log x+5x$.

At $x=e$, $\log e=1$, so $y''=6e+5e=11e$.
blocks.answer: $y''=6x\log x+5x$, and its value at $x=e$ is $11e$

blocks.solution:
$y'=e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$.

$y''=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)+e^x(\cos x-\sin x)=2e^x\cos x$.

Then $y''-2y'+2y=2e^x\cos x-2e^x\sin x-2e^x\cos x+2e^x\sin x=0$.
blocks.answer: The relation is verified: it equals $0$

blocks.text: **Parametric form.** If $x=\phi(t)$ and $y=\psi(t)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$ and the second derivative is found by differentiating $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ with respect to $t$ and dividing again by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$.
Valid when $dx/dt\neq0$. Do **not** take $\dfrac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}$; that is wrong.
**Implicit form.** Differentiate the relation with respect to $x$ treating $y$ as a function of $x$, solve for $y'$, then differentiate again, substituting $y'$ back.
Second derivative is **not** the square of the first derivative: $y''\neq(y')^2$. Keep the product and chain rules in view when differentiating the first derivative.

On an interval $I$, $f$ is **increasing** if $x_1<x_2\Rightarrow f(x_1)\le f(x_2)$ (strictly increasing if $<$), and **decreasing** if $x_1<x_2\Rightarrow f(x_1)\ge f(x_2)$ (strictly decreasing if $>$).

If $f$ is differentiable on an interval, then $f'(x)\ge0$ for all $x$ in the interval means $f$ is increasing there, and $f'(x)\le0$ means $f$ is decreasing. If $f'(x)>0$ throughout, $f$ is strictly increasing. A function is also increasing if $f'\ge0$ and $f'=0$ only at isolated points.

**Method.** (1) Find $f'(x)$. (2) Solve $f'(x)=0$ to get the points that divide the line into intervals. (3) Find the sign of $f'$ in each interval. Positive means increasing; negative means decreasing.

blocks.problem: Find the intervals in which $f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+5$ is increasing or decreasing.
blocks.solution:
$f'(x)=6x^2-18x+12=6(x-1)(x-2)$, which is zero at $x=1$ and $x=2$.

For $x<1$ both factors are negative, so $f'>0$. For $1<x<2$, $(x-1)>0$ and $(x-2)<0$, so $f'<0$. For $x>2$, $f'>0$.
$f'(x)=3x^2-6x+3=3(x-1)^2\ge0$ for all $x$, and $f'(x)=0$ only at $x=1$. So $f$ is increasing on the whole real line, even though its slope is momentarily 0 at $x=1$.

blocks.problem: Find the least value of $a$ for which $f(x)=x^2+ax+1$ is increasing on $[1,2]$.
blocks.solution:
$f'(x)=2x+a$. We need $2x+a\ge0$ for all $x\in[1,2]$. The smallest value of $2x+a$ on the interval is at $x=1$: $2+a$.

So $2+a\ge0$, i.e. $a\ge-2$.

blocks.text: Do not test increasing/decreasing from a couple of values. Use the sign of $f'$ on each interval between the roots of $f'=0$.

$f$ has a **local maximum** at $c$ if $f(c)\ge f(x)$ for all $x$ near $c$, and a **local minimum** if $f(c)\le f(x)$ for all $x$ near $c$. Points where $f'(c)=0$ (or $f'$ does not exist) are called **critical points**.

blocks.caption: Tests for local extrema
rows: Test fails; use the first derivative test

blocks.problem: Find the local maximum and local minimum values of $f(x)=x^3-3x$.
blocks.answer: Local maximum value $2$ at $x=-1$; local minimum value $-2$ at $x=1$

blocks.problem: Find the local maximum and local minimum values of $f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+1$.
blocks.answer: Local maximum $29$ at $x=2$; local minimum $28$ at $x=3$

blocks.term: Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
blocks.text: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, its absolute maximum and minimum occur at the critical points inside $(a,b)$ or at the end points. Compute $f$ at each and compare.

blocks.problem: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of $f(x)=x^3-3x^2$ on $[-2,3]$.
blocks.solution:
$f'(x)=3x^2-6x=3x(x-2)$, so the critical points are $0$ and $2$ (both inside the interval).

$f(-2)=-8-12=-20$, $f(0)=0$, $f(2)=8-12=-4$, $f(3)=27-27=0$.

The largest is $0$ and the smallest is $-20$.

blocks.problem: A farmer has 200 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river; no fence is needed along the river. Find the maximum area.
blocks.solution:
Let the two sides perpendicular to the river have length $x$ and the side parallel to it $y$. Then $2x+y=200$, so $y=200-2x$.

Area $A=x(200-2x)=200x-2x^2$. $A'=200-4x=0\Rightarrow x=50$, $y=100$. $A''=-4<0$, so this is a maximum.

$A=50\times100=5000$.

blocks.problem: A square sheet of side 12 cm has a square of side $x$ cut from each corner and is folded into an open box. Find the maximum volume.

blocks.text: A local maximum value can be smaller than a local minimum value of the same function (for example $f(x)=x+\tfrac1x$ has local maximum $-2$ at $x=-1$ and local minimum $2$ at $x=1$). Also, $f''(c)=0$ does not tell you there is no extremum.

Steps for word problems: define the variable, form a function of one variable, find critical points, check with the second derivative, state the answer with units. Check the end points when the domain is closed.

questions.stem: If $y=x^4-3x^2+5$, then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $x=1$ is
questions.explanation: $y'=4x^3-6x$, so $y''=12x^2-6$. At $x=1$, $y''=12-6=6$. The value $-2$ would be the first derivative $4-6$ at $x=1$.

optionRationale.3: This is the coefficient $12$ of $x^2$ in $y''$ without the constant $-6$.
optionRationale.4: No correct step gives this value.

questions.objective: Find a second derivative of a polynomial

questions.stem: If $y=e^{2x}$, the value of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $x=0$ is
questions.explanation: $y'=2e^{2x}$ and $y''=4e^{2x}$. At $x=0$, $e^0=1$, so $y''=4$. Each differentiation multiplies by the constant 2. So $y'=2e^{2x}$ first, then $y''=2\cdot2e^{2x}$, and $e^{0}=1$.

optionRationale.1: This is the first derivative at $x=0$.

questions.objective: Differentiate an exponential function twice

questions.stem: If $y=\sin3x$, then $\dfrac{y''}{y}$ equals
questions.explanation: $y'=3\cos3x$ and $y''=-9\sin3x=-9y$, so $y''/y=-9$. This is the standard relation $y''+9y=0$ for simple harmonic type functions.

optionRationale.1: This would be the case only for the first derivative's factor.
optionRationale.2: The sign is wrong; the second derivative of a sine is negative.
optionRationale.4: Neither the magnitude nor the sign is correct.

questions.objective: Relate y'' to y for a sine function

questions.stem: If $y=x^3\log x$, then the value of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $x=e$ is
questions.explanation: $y'=3x^2\log x+x^2$ by the product rule. Then $y''=6x\log x+3x+2x=6x\log x+5x$. At $x=e$, $\log e=1$, so $y''=6e+5e=11e$.
questions.objective: Apply the product rule twice

questions.stem: If $x=t^2$ and $y=t^3$ with $t>0$, then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $t=2$ is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3t^2}{2t}=\dfrac{3t}2$. Then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{3t}2\right)\Big/\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{3/2}{2t}=\dfrac3{4t}$. At $t=2$ this is $\dfrac38$.
questions.objective: Find a second derivative of a parametric function

questions.stem: If $x=a\cos\theta$ and $y=a\sin\theta$, then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$ is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{a\cos\theta}{-a\sin\theta}=-\cot\theta$. Then $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(-\cot\theta)=\csc^2\theta$, and dividing by $dx/d\theta=-a\sin\theta$ gives $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac1{a\sin^3\theta}$. At $\theta=\pi/2$ this equals $-\dfrac1a$.

optionRationale.1: The sign is wrong; the circle is concave down at the top.
optionRationale.3: This is $dy/dx$ at $\theta=\pi/2$, not the second derivative.

questions.objective: Second derivative of a circle in parametric form

questions.stem: For the curve $x^2+y^2=25$, the value of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at the point $(3,4)$ is
questions.explanation: $y'=-x/y$. Then $y''=-\dfrac{y-xy'}{y^2}=-\dfrac{y+x^2/y}{y^2}=-\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{y^3}=-\dfrac{25}{y^3}$. At $(3,4)$: $-\dfrac{25}{64}$. It is negative, since the upper half of the circle is concave down.

optionRationale.4: Uses $y^2$ instead of $y^3$ in the denominator.

questions.objective: Second derivative of an implicit function

questions.stem: If $y=e^x\sin x$, then $y''-2y'+2y$ equals
questions.explanation: $y'=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$ and $y''=2e^x\cos x$. Then $y''-2y'+2y=2e^x\cos x-2e^x\sin x-2e^x\cos x+2e^x\sin x=0$.

optionRationale.2: Only the last two terms were added.
optionRationale.3: Sign errors in the middle term.

questions.objective: Verify a differential relation using second derivatives

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is increasing for all real $x$?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x>0$ for all $x$, so $e^x$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$. The derivative of $x^2$ is negative for $x<0$, that of $-2x+1$ is always negative, and $\sin x$ changes direction.

optionRationale.3: Its derivative is $-2<0$, so it is decreasing.

questions.objective: Identify an increasing function using the derivative

questions.stem: The function $f(x)=x^2-6x+8$ is strictly decreasing in the interval
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=2x-6$, which is negative when $x<3$ and positive when $x>3$. So $f$ is strictly decreasing in $(-\infty,3)$ and increasing in $(3,\infty)$. The vertex of the parabola at $x=3$ is the turning point where the slope changes sign.

optionRationale.4: The sign of the critical point is wrong.

questions.objective: Find the interval of decrease of a quadratic

questions.stem: The cubic $f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+5$ falls only between two consecutive roots of $f'(x)$. That open interval is
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=6x^2-18x+12=6(x-1)(x-2)$. Between the roots, $x-1>0$ and $x-2<0$, so $f'<0$. Hence $f$ is strictly decreasing in $(1,2)$ and increasing elsewhere.

optionRationale.4: This does not contain the roots 1 and 2 of $f'$.

questions.objective: Use the sign of the derivative to find intervals of monotonicity

questions.stem: The function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+3x-5$ is
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=3x^2-6x+3=3(x-1)^2$, which is non-negative for all $x$ and zero only at $x=1$. A function whose derivative is non-negative, vanishing only at an isolated point, is increasing on the whole line.
questions.objective: Recognise an increasing function with a stationary point

questions.stem: The least value of $a$ for which $f(x)=x^2+ax+1$ is increasing on $[1,2]$ is
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=2x+a$ must be $\ge0$ for every $x\in[1,2]$. Its smallest value on the interval is at $x=1$, namely $2+a$. So $2+a\ge0$ and $a\ge-2$. The least value is $-2$.

optionRationale.3: This would come from $f'(2)=4+a\ge0$, which is a weaker condition at the other end.
optionRationale.4: This is the condition $f'\ge0$ at $x=0$, not on $[1,2]$.

questions.objective: Find a parameter for which a function is increasing

questions.stem: The local minimum value of $f(x)=x^2-4x+7$ is
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=2x-4=0$ gives $x=2$ and $f''=2>0$, so it is a minimum. The value is $f(2)=4-8+7=3$. This agrees with completing the square: $x^2-4x+7=(x-2)^2+3\ge3$.

optionRationale.1: This is the point $x=2$ where the minimum occurs, not its value.

questions.objective: Find a local minimum value of a quadratic

questions.stem: The local maximum value of $f(x)=x^3-3x$ is
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=3x^2-3=0$ gives $x=\pm1$ and $f''=6x$. At $x=-1$, $f''=-6<0$, so there is a local maximum of $f(-1)=-1+3=2$. At $x=1$ there is a local minimum of $-2$.

optionRationale.1: This is the local minimum value at $x=1$.
optionRationale.2: This comes from a sign slip when evaluating $f(-1)$.
optionRationale.3: This is $f(0)$, which is not an extremum.

questions.objective: Find a local maximum value using the second derivative test

questions.stem: For $f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+1$, the difference (local maximum value) $-$ (local minimum value) is

optionRationale.2: This comes from a wrong value of one extremum; the values are 29 and 28.
optionRationale.3: The order of subtraction is reversed.
optionRationale.4: This is the sum of the two extremum values.

questions.objective: Compare local extremum values of a cubic

questions.stem: For $f(x)=x^3-3x^2$ on $[-2,3]$, if $M$ is the absolute maximum and $m$ the absolute minimum, then $M-m$ equals
questions.explanation: $f'(x)=3x(x-2)$, so critical points are 0 and 2. The values are $f(-2)=-20$, $f(0)=0$, $f(2)=-4$, $f(3)=0$. So $M=0$, $m=-20$ and $M-m=20$. The end point $x=-2$ gives the minimum.

optionRationale.1: This is $0-(-4)$, using the local minimum $-4$ instead of the absolute minimum.

questions.objective: Find absolute extrema on a closed interval

questions.stem: A farmer has 200 m of fencing and encloses a rectangular field with a river forming one side, so that only three sides need fencing. The maximum area is
questions.explanation: Let the sides perpendicular to the river be $x$ and the side along the river be $200-2x$. Then $A=x(200-2x)$, $A'=200-4x=0$ gives $x=50$ and $A''=-4<0$. The maximum area is $50\times100=5000$ m².

optionRationale.1: This is the area $50\times50$, which does not use the fencing correctly.
optionRationale.2: This is $100\times100$, which would need 300 m of fencing.

questions.objective: Solve an applied maximum problem

questions.stem: A square sheet of side 12 cm has equal squares of side $x$ cut from its corners and is folded to form an open box. The maximum volume of the box is
questions.explanation: $V=x(12-2x)^2=4x^3-48x^2+144x$. $V'=12(x-2)(x-6)$ gives $x=2$ in $(0,6)$, and $V''(2)=-48<0$ confirms a maximum. $V(2)=2\times8^2=128$ cm³. At $x=3$ the volume is $3\times36=108$, which is smaller.

optionRationale.1: At $x=6$ there is no base left, so the volume is 0; 144 is not obtained from any admissible $x$.
optionRationale.2: Obtained with $x=3$, which is not the maximum.
optionRationale.3: Obtained by doubling the correct answer.

questions.objective: Maximise the volume of an open box

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements for a function $f$ with $f'(c)=0$.
A. If $f''(c)<0$, then $f$ has a local maximum at $c$.
B. If $f''(c)>0$, then $f$ has a local minimum at $c$.
C. If $f''(c)=0$, then $f$ has neither a maximum nor a minimum at $c$.
D. A local maximum value of a function can be less than a local minimum value of the same function.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A and B are the second derivative test. C is false: $f(x)=x^4$ has $f''(0)=0$ yet a minimum at 0, so the test is merely inconclusive. D is true: $x+1/x$ has local maximum $-2$ at $x=-1$ and local minimum $2$ at $x=1$.

optionRationale.2: D is also true, so this option is incomplete.
optionRationale.3: C is false, since $f(x)=x^4$ has a minimum at 0 although $f''(0)=0$.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so any option containing C is wrong.

questions.objective: Recall the conditions of the second derivative test

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The function $f(x)=x^3$ has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum, although $f'(0)=0$.
Reason (R): The derivative $f'(x)=3x^2$ does not change sign at $x=0$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A critical point gives a local extremum only if $f'$ changes sign there. Here $f'=3x^2\ge0$ on both sides of 0, so the function keeps increasing through $x=0$. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: The reason is exactly what prevents an extremum at 0, so it is the correct explanation.
optionRationale.3: The assertion is true: $x^3$ is increasing on the whole line.
optionRationale.4: The reason is true: $3x^2$ is non-negative on both sides of 0.

questions.objective: Explain why a critical point need not be an extremum

questions.stem: Match the function in List-I with the property in List-II.
questions.explanation: $f=x^3+x$ has $f'=3x^2+1>0$, so it is increasing (I). $f=x^2-2x$ has $f'=2x-2=0$ at $x=1$ and $f''=2>0$, so a minimum (II). $f=-x^2-2x$ has $f'=-2x-2=0$ at $x=-1$ and $f''=-2<0$, so a maximum (III). $f=e^{-x}$ has $f'=-e^{-x}<0$, so it is decreasing (IV).

optionRationale.2: $x^3+x$ is increasing, not a quadratic with a minimum, so A-II is wrong.
optionRationale.3: The quadratic $x^2-2x$ has a minimum, not a maximum, so B-III is wrong.
optionRationale.4: $-x^2-2x$ has a maximum at $-1$ and $e^{-x}$ is decreasing, so C-IV and D-III are swapped.

questions.objective: Match functions with monotonicity and extremum properties

right: II. Has a local minimum at $x=1$
III. Has a local maximum at $x=-1$
